name: Afro

card.summary: A rounded, voluminous hairstyle made by letting tightly coiled natural hair grow out and shaping it into a dome, adding head volume and a bold silhouette.
card.note: Afro-textured hair is prone to breakage; heavy styling tension and backcombing can damage hair and scalp.

quick.overview:
The Afro is a rounded hairstyle in which naturally coiled, kinky hair is grown out and shaped outward from the scalp into a dome. It adds head volume and height, frames the face, and shows natural texture instead of straightening it.

It rose in the mid-1960s alongside the Black is beautiful movement and has been revived repeatedly since. Hair-science studies of Afro-textured hair focus on breakage and styling damage, which shapes how care is discussed.
quick.how: People grow out natural hair, then lift and shape it from the roots with a wide-toothed pick to form the round outline. Length and density set the size; some cut it into a mini-afro or tapered shape. Moisture and gentle handling are the usual themes of care, and styles like braids and weaves can alternate with it.
quick.risks: Studies find Afro-textured hair breaks more readily under repeated stress, and traction alopecia is common among women who wear extensions, wigs and tight braids. Backcombing for extra volume could harm hair and scalp according to Wikipedia. Wearing the style in some workplaces and schools has drawn discrimination, which some US states have legislated against.

lead: The Afro is a hairstyle in which tightly coiled, natural hair is grown out and shaped into a rounded form radiating from the scalp. Its name comes from Afro-American, and it is also called a natural. It emerged in the mid-1960s and became a symbol of Black pride during the civil rights era. [1][2]

For appearance, it adds volume and height, creates a rounded silhouette that frames the face, and lets people wear their natural texture without chemical straightening. It can be maintained largely at home, which made it more accessible than salon-dependent relaxed styles or braids. [1][2]

Hair-science research on Afro-textured hair studies how it responds to grooming. Studies describe higher breakage under repeated stress than in other hair types and associate frequent braiding, extensions and chemical relaxing with fibre damage and traction alopecia. [3][4][5][6]

chain: Lift and shape outward with a pick
Rounded dome adds volume and head height
Bold framing silhouette around the face
angle.text: The style uses the hair's own coil to create volume, so the hair itself changes the outline of the head. Size is set by length and density, and shaping is done with a wide-toothed pick.

infobox: Angela Davis, Pam Grier, Jimi Hendrix, Jackson 5

paras: Afro-textured hair tends to grow outward as it lengthens, producing a dome that can be shaped with a wide-toothed pick. For wavy or straight hair, chemical products or setting liquids are used to hold a similar shape. [2]

Grokipedia describes the style as dependent on type 4 hair, subtypes 4A to 4C, and describes mini-afro and other sub-styles; that source is AI-generated and its details have not been confirmed against other references. [1]

Before the 1960s many African Americans straightened their hair with chemical relaxers or wore braids and cornrows. The Afro emerged in the mid-1960s, including among Black Panther Party members, and was linked to the Civil Rights Movement and the Black is beautiful movement as a symbol of pride and a rejection of assimilation. It grew larger in the late 1960s and early 1970s, with Angela Davis, Pam Grier, Jimi Hendrix, Miriam Makeba, the Jackson 5 and the Supremes among well-known wearers. [2]

Its popularity among African Americans waned by the early 1970s as mainstream adoption lessened its political edge and cornrows and braids grew more common. It returned in the 1990s and 2000s in varied forms, including twists, close-cropped cuts and large wigs. [2]

The style also carried contested meanings. Some African nationalists viewed its adoption by African Americans as Western arrogance, and Tanzania banned it in the 1970s as a neocolonial cultural invasion. [2]
A 2009 fatigue-testing study reported a substantially higher tendency to breakage in Afro hair than Caucasian hair, with relative humidity a significant factor. [3]

A 2021 study in Johannesburg compared 15 frequent braiders with 15 occasional braiders using electron microscopy and tensile tests, noting that Afro hair breakage is commonly attributed to braiding, extensions and weaves but that quantitative data had been scarce. [4] A 2019 microscopy study of 96 Ghanaian women compared natural (Afro), braided or woven, and chemically relaxed hair. [5]

In a cross-sectional study at salons in Yaounde, Cameroon, 34.5 percent of 223 women had traction alopecia and 95.1 percent regularly used extensions. [6] Wikipedia notes that some people gain volume by backcombing, which can harm hair and scalp. [2]

Studies concern hair structure and styling-related damage rather than treatments or appearance outcomes. The key findings are the Johannesburg braiding study, [4] the Ghana microscopy study, [5] the Cameroon traction alopecia survey, [6] and the fatigue-testing study. [3]
On July 3, 2019, California became the first US state to ban discrimination based on natural hair through the CROWN Act, and New York passed a similar law later that year. [2]

timeline.event: The Afro emerges in the United States, including among Black Panther Party members. [2]
Afros grow larger and become widely worn. [2]
The style is revived in varied forms. [2]
California passes the CROWN Act on July 3, followed by New York. [2]
